docs.title: PIVPy data model (xarray)
docs.text: PIVPy's core data structure is an xarray.Dataset. This page explains how it is organized, how to access values correctly, which metadata is typically stored, and how this compares conceptually to PIVMat "structures" and "structure arrays".

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A typical vector PIV dataset contains:

  • dimensions: ('y', 'x', 't')
  • coordinates: 1D x, 1D y, 1D t
  • data variables: u, v and chc (and sometimes mask)

A typical scalar dataset contains:

  • dimensions: usually ('y', 'x', 't') (or ('y', 'x') for single images)
  • data variable: w (plus optionally chc/mask)

The recommended way to interact with PIVPy datasets is via the xarray accessor:

import pivpy.pivpy  # registers the Dataset.piv accessor
from pivpy import io

ds = io.read_piv("B00001.VC7")
ds.piv.showf()

docs.title: Single vector field
docs.text: A single field is typically represented as a dataset with t of length 1 (or sometimes without t, depending on the reader and context).

docs.title: Common data variables
docs.text: Name Type / dims Meaning u float, (y, x, t) x-component of velocity (or displacement) v float, (y, x, t) y-component of velocity (or displacement) chc int/bool, (y, x, t) validity / choice / quality flag (reader-dependent) mask (optional) int/bool, (y, x, t) mask information if present in the source export

docs.title: Common coordinates
docs.text: Name Type / dims Meaning x float, (x,) x-coordinate of grid points (physical units) y float, (y,) y-coordinate of grid points (physical units) t float/int, (t,) time coordinate (frames or physical time, depends on loader)

docs.title: Units and labels
docs.text:
PIVPy stores units/labels using xarray attributes:

  • ds['x'].attrs.get('units')
  • ds['y'].attrs.get('units')
  • ds['u'].attrs.get('units')
  • ds['v'].attrs.get('units')

Example:

x_units = ds["x"].attrs.get("units", "")
u_units = ds["u"].attrs.get("units", "")

docs.title: Single scalar field
docs.text:
Scalar fields (images or derived scalars like vorticity) usually use w:

Name Type / dims Meaning w float, (y, x, t) or (y, x) scalar field values (e.g. vorticity, divergence, intensity)

Scalar datasets are often produced using vec2scal:

import pivpy.pivpy

vort = ds.piv.vec2scal("vorticity", name="w")
vort.piv.showf(scalar="w")

docs.title: Time series ("array of fields")
docs.text: In PIVMat, a "structure array" stores many fields as a 1D array of structs. In PIVPy, the usual equivalent is a single xarray.Dataset where multiple frames are stacked along the t dimension.

docs.title: Inspecting shape
docs.text:
ds.dims
ds.sizes  # contains sizes for y/x/t

docs.title: Selecting frames
docs.text:
first = ds.isel(t=0)
one_frame = ds.isel(t=5)
subset = ds.isel(t=slice(0, 10))

docs.title: Indexing and coordinate conventions
docs.text:
xarray uses NumPy-like indexing: arrays stored as (y, x, t) mean:

  • axis 0 is y (rows)
  • axis 1 is x (columns)
  • axis 2 is time

So the element access is:

# value at y-index iy, x-index ix, time-index it
val = ds["u"].values[iy, ix, it]

Coordinate-based selection is also available:

# select nearest physical coordinate
pt = ds.sel(x=10.0, y=20.0, method="nearest")

docs.title: Plotting conventions
docs.text:
PIVPy plotting helpers are designed to respect coordinate arrays. For example:

import pivpy.pivpy

ds.isel(t=0).piv.showf(background="vorticity")

docs.title: About "ysign"
docs.text: PIVMat stores a dedicated ysign string to track upward vs downward y-axis. PIVPy generally relies on the ordering of the coordinate arrays y and x. The plotting functions in pivpy.graphics handle flipped axes by inspecting the coordinate ordering.

docs.title: Metadata (attrs)
docs.text:
PIVPy stores dataset-level metadata in ds.attrs. Not every reader populates the same keys, but you will often see entries like:

  • name: file name
  • setname: directory / set identifier
  • source: origin/format
  • delta_t: time step (when known)
  • history: list of processing steps (PIVMat-like concept)

Example:

ds.attrs
ds.attrs.get("history", [])

Many PIVPy operations append to ds.attrs['history'] (when the function is written in the PIVMat-compat style).

docs.title: DaVis / vendor attributes
docs.text:
PIVMat stores vendor metadata in a big string field called Attributes and uses functions like getattribute to parse it.

In PIVPy, vendor-specific metadata may appear either:

  • in ds.attrs as structured keys, or
  • as separate variables/attributes (reader-dependent)

The convenience functions in pivpy.io and the accessor methods in pivpy.pivpy.PIVAccessor are the recommended way to work with those details.

docs.title: Show the dataset "layout"
docs.text:
import pivpy.pivpy
from pivpy import io

ds = io.read_piv("B00001.VC7")

print(ds)
print("dims:", ds.dims)
print("vars:", list(ds.data_vars))
print("coords:", list(ds.coords))

docs.title: Compute a derived scalar with consistent units
docs.text:
vort = ds.piv.vec2scal("vorticity", name="w")
print(vort["w"].attrs.get("units", ""))

docs.title: Track processing history
docs.text:
ds2 = ds.piv.filterf(1.0, "gauss")
ds2 = ds2.piv.vec2scal("vorticity", name="w")
print(ds2.attrs.get("history", []))

docs.title: PIVPy FAQ
docs.text:
This page is a practical, example-driven FAQ for common PIVPy workflows. It is inspired by the kind of questions users ask when coming from MATLAB toolboxes, but the snippets below use real PIVPy functions and the xarray-based PIVPy data model.

Most examples assume you have installed optional dependencies if you need them (e.g. lvpyio for LaVision .vc7).

docs.title: How do I import and display velocity fields?
docs.text:
Load a single file (format auto-detected) and display it:

import pivpy.pivpy  # registers the Dataset.piv accessor
from pivpy import io

ds = io.read_piv("B00001.VC7")
ds.piv.showf()  # vector field

Load many files (directory / glob) and display the first frame:

ds = io.loadvec("*.VC7")  # or io.read_directory("path/to/dir")
ds.isel(t=0).piv.showf()

docs.title: How do I get quick help on a PIVPy function?
docs.text:
In Python you can use help() (or IPython ?):

import pivpy
from pivpy import io

help(io.read_piv)
help(io.loadvec)

For API-level docs, see API reference.

docs.title: My velocity fields are noisy. How do I smooth them?
docs.text:
Two common choices:

  1. A spatial convolution filter (Gaussian / kernel-based), similar in spirit to PIVMat's filtering:
import pivpy.pivpy
from pivpy import io

ds = io.read_piv("B00001.VC7")
ds_smooth = ds.piv.filterf(1.0, "gauss")
ds_smooth.piv.showf()
  1. A frequency-domain Butterworth filter:
ds_low = ds.piv.bwfilterf(filtsize=3.0, order=8.0, mode="low")
ds_low.piv.showf()

If you specifically want a temporal running average over frames, use smoothf:

from pivpy.compute_funcs import smoothf

ds_smoothed_in_time = smoothf(ds, n=5)

docs.title: How do I display vorticity from a velocity field?
docs.text:
Option A: compute a scalar field and display it:

import pivpy.pivpy
from pivpy import io

ds = io.read_piv("B00001.VC7")
vort = ds.piv.vec2scal("vorticity", name="w")
vort.piv.showf(scalar="w")

Option B: use a scalar background behind the vectors:

ds.piv.showf(background="vorticity")

docs.title: I only want to view the first N frames
docs.text:
With a time-series dataset, select a slice on t:

ds10 = ds.isel(t=slice(0, 10))
ds10.isel(t=0).piv.showf()

To create a quick movie (mp4/gif depending on your Matplotlib/ffmpeg setup):

ds10.piv.to_movie("preview.mp4", background="vorticity")

docs.title: Can I import IMX/IM7 image files?
docs.text:
PIVPy includes readers for several formats; availability depends on optional dependencies. If you have .imx/.im7 support in your environment, you can load them as scalar datasets and display them:

import pivpy.pivpy
from pivpy import io

img = io.openim7("frame.im7")
img.piv.showf(scalar="w", cmap="gray")

docs.title: Can I import vector fields saved in TXT/DAT?
docs.text:
Yes. If you have OpenPIV/ASCII-like exports:

import pivpy.pivpy
from pivpy import io

ds = io.load_openpiv_txt("field.txt")
ds.piv.showf()

docs.title: Why aren't all vectors displayed?
docs.text:
By default, dense fields can look unreadable. You can subsample arrows in the quiver plot using nthArr (plot every Nth vector in each direction):

ds.piv.showf(nthArr=3)

docs.title: What's the relationship between LaVision's ReadIMX and PIVPy?
docs.text: PIVPy can use lvpyio (when installed) to read LaVision VC7/IMX/IM7 content. PIVPy then stores the result in a consistent xarray.Dataset and provides processing/plotting via the Dataset.piv accessor.

docs.title: How do I plot iso-lines (contours) of a scalar property?
docs.text:
Compute a scalar (e.g., velocity magnitude) and use Matplotlib contours:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pivpy.pivpy

mag = ds.piv.vec2scal("norm", name="w")
w = np.asarray(mag["w"].isel(t=0).values)

X, Y = np.meshgrid(mag["x"].values, mag["y"].values)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.contourf(X, Y, w, levels=15)
ax.set_aspect("equal")

docs.title: How do I "navigate" through frames?
docs.text:
Because fields are stored as an xarray time series, you can index frames with isel:

frame = ds.isel(t=5)
frame.piv.showf(background="vorticity")

Or iterate:

for ti in range(ds.sizes["t"]):
    ds.isel(t=ti).piv.showf()

docs.title: How are fields stored in PIVPy?
docs.text:
PIVPy's core structure is an xarray.Dataset with:

  • dimensions: ('y', 'x', 't')
  • coordinates: x, y, t
  • variables: usually u, v, and chc (validity)

Example:

list(ds.dims)
list(ds.data_vars)
ds

docs.title: How do I plot a velocity profile or a vorticity profile?
docs.text:
Pick a line index and plot with Matplotlib:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

j = 12  # y-index
uline = ds["u"].isel(t=0, y=j)
plt.plot(ds["x"], uline)
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("u")

For a vorticity profile:

vort = ds.piv.vec2scal("vorticity", name="w")
wline = vort["w"].isel(t=0, y=j)
plt.plot(vort["x"], wline)

docs.title: How do I plot a spatio-temporal diagram?
docs.text:
Build a matrix where x is one axis and time is the other:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

j = 12
d = np.asarray(ds["u"].isel(y=j).values).T  # shape (t, x)

plt.figure()
plt.imshow(d, aspect="auto", origin="lower")
plt.xlabel("x-index")
plt.ylabel("t-index")

Or, for a PIVMat-style spatio-temporal correlation on a scalar series, use spatiotempcorrf:

from pivpy.compute_funcs import spatiotempcorrf

scalar = ds.piv.vec2scal("vorticity", name="w")
cor = spatiotempcorrf(scalar)

docs.title: How do I see the list of operations applied to a field?
docs.text:
Many PIVPy operations append entries to ds.attrs['history'].

ds2 = ds.piv.filterf(1.0, "gauss")
ds2.attrs.get("history", [])

docs.title: I have hundreds/thousands of fields and can't keep them all in memory
docs.text:
If your workflow can be expressed as "load a file → process → reduce/save", use batchf:

from pivpy.io import batchf

# Apply an accessor method to each file and collect results
results = batchf("*.VC7", "averf")

For custom logic, iterate over filenames and process one at a time.

docs.title: How do I save processed fields?
docs.text:
Common choices:

  • NetCDF via xarray:
ds.to_netcdf("processed.nc")
  • MATLAB .mat export helper for interoperability:
from pivpy.io import vec2mat

vec2mat(ds, "processed.mat")

docs.title: How do I compute RMS over a time series?
docs.text:
averf can return average, std, and rms:

avg, std, rms = ds.piv.averf(return_std_rms=True)
rms.piv.showf(background=None)

docs.title: PIVPy tutorial
docs.text: This tutorial is a practical, code-first walkthrough of common PIVPy workflows. It focuses on the xarray-based API and several PIVMAT-inspired helpers.

docs.title: Install pivpy
docs.text:
Recommended (fast, reproducible):

uv venv
uv pip install pivpy

Or with optional dependencies:

uv pip install 'pivpy[full]'

docs.title: Load a dataset
docs.text:
PIVPy's main object is an xarray.Dataset. Most post-processing is exposed via the accessor ds.piv.

import pivpy.pivpy  # registers the .piv accessor
from pivpy import io

ds = io.read_piv('your_file.vec')

Typical dataset structure:

  • Dims: ('y', 'x', 't')
  • Variables: u, v, and (often) chc

docs.title: Create a scalar dataset from an image (PIVMAT-style im2pivmat)
docs.text:
If you have a 2D image array (shape (y, x)), you can wrap it into a PIVPy scalar Dataset using pivpy.io.im2pivmat:

import numpy as np
from pivpy import io
import pivpy.pivpy  # registers the .piv accessor

im = np.random.rand(128, 256)
ds_im = io.im2pivmat(im, namew='I', unit='au')

# Plot the scalar field
ds_im.piv.showscal(property='w')

docs.title: Save animations (PIVMAT-style showf / imvectomovie)
docs.text:
PIVPy can render a Dataset as a movie efficiently by creating the Matplotlib artists once and updating them frame-by-frame (fast renderer).

In-memory Dataset (uses the t dimension as frames):

import pivpy.pivpy  # registers the .piv accessor
from pivpy import io

ds = io.create_sample_Dataset(n_frames=20)

# Write a movie (requires FFmpeg for mp4/avi)
ds.piv.to_movie('movie.mp4', fps=10, show='vector', nthArr=2, scalingFactor=10.0)

# Or collect frames as RGBA arrays (no external encoders required)
frames = ds.piv.to_movie(None, return_frames=True, show='vector')

Streaming from disk (loads files one-by-one, PIVMAT imvectomovie-style):

from pivpy import graphics

# Convert many files to a movie without loading all of them into RAM
graphics.imvectomovie('data/*.vc7', 'movie.mp4', fps=10, show='vector', nthArr=3)

Notes:

  • Writing .mp4/.avi uses Matplotlib's FFmpeg writer (FFmpeg must be installed).
  • Writing .gif uses Matplotlib's Pillow writer (Pillow must be installed).
  • Use show='scalar' and scalar='w' to render scalar-only datasets.

docs.title: Interpolate missing data (PIVMAT-style interpf)
docs.text:
PIVMAT's interpf fills missing values (0 or NaN) inside fields. In PIVPy this is available as:

import pivpy.pivpy  # registers the .piv accessor
from pivpy import io

ds = io.create_sample_Dataset(n_frames=5)
ds_filled = ds.piv.interpf(method=0)  # Laplacian inpainting (smooth)

# Faster options:
ds_nn = ds.piv.interpf(method=1)      # nearest-neighbor
ds_lin = ds.piv.interpf(method=2)     # linear + nearest fallback

# Control what is considered "missing":
ds_nan_only = ds.piv.interpf(method=1, missing='nan')
ds_zero_only = ds.piv.interpf(method=1, missing='0')

docs.title: Joint PDF of two scalar fields (PIVMAT-style jpdfscal)
docs.text:
You can compute a joint histogram ("joint PDF" in PIVMAT terminology) of two scalar variables and display it with filled contours:

import pivpy.pivpy  # registers the .piv accessor
from pivpy import io

ds = io.create_sample_Dataset(n_frames=10)
ds = ds.piv.vec2scal('vorticity', name='w')
ds = ds.piv.vec2scal('divergence', name='div')

jpdf = ds.piv.jpdfscal('w', 'div', nbin=101)
fig, ax = ds.piv.jpdfscal_disp('w', 'div', nbin=101)

docs.title: Probe time series (PIVMAT-style probef and probeaverf)
docs.text:
Sample the time evolution at a point (with bilinear interpolation):

p = ds.piv.probef(20.0, 30.0, variables=['u', 'v'])
# p['u'] and p['v'] are 1D time series over the dataset's t dimension

Average over a rectangular probe area [x1, y1, x2, y2]:

pavg = ds.piv.probeaverf([10.0, 10.0, 30.0, 40.0], variables=['u', 'v'])

docs.title: Spatio-temporal diagram (PIVMAT-style spatiotempf)
docs.text:
Sample a scalar field along a line segment for each time frame:

ds = ds.piv.vec2scal('vorticity', name='w')
st = ds.piv.spatiotempf([0.0, 50.0], [10.0, 10.0], var='w', n=200)
# st['st'] has dims (t, s) and can be plotted with imshow/pcolormesh.

docs.title: Temporal correlation (PIVMAT-style tempcorrf)
docs.text:
Compute the temporal correlation function f(T) of a scalar (or vector) time series averaged over space:

cor = ds.piv.tempcorrf(variables=['w'], normalize=True)
# cor['f'] is the correlation vs lag cor['t']

docs.title: Gradient of a scalar field (PIVMAT-style gradientf)
docs.text:
Compute the gradient of any scalar variable (for example a vorticity field stored in ds['w']). The result is a new Dataset with vector components stored as u and v:

import pivpy.pivpy  # registers the .piv accessor
from pivpy import io

ds = io.create_sample_Dataset(n_frames=1)
ds = ds.piv.vec2scal('vorticity', name='w')

grad = ds.piv.gradientf(variable='w')
# grad contains grad['u'] = dw/dx and grad['v'] = dw/dy

You can plot it like any other vector field:

grad.piv.showf()

docs.title: Histogram of a field (PIVMAT-style histf)
docs.text:
Compute a histogram for a scalar field (values are stacked over the full field and all time frames):

h = ds.piv.histf(variable='w')
# h is a Dataset with coordinate h['bin'] and counts h['h']

By default, zeros are treated as invalid and excluded. To include zeros, pass opt='0':

h0 = ds.piv.histf(variable='w', opt='0')

Vector mode (no variable specified) computes histograms for both components of the velocity field:

hv = ds.piv.histf()
# hv contains hv['hx'] for u (or vx) and hv['hy'] for v (or vy)

docs.title: Graphical histogram display (PIVMAT-style)
docs.text:
PIVPy also includes plotting helpers inspired by PIVMAT's histscal_disp and histvec_disp.

Scalar histogram display (with optional PDF normalization):

from pivpy import graphics

fig, ax = graphics.histscal_disp(ds, variable='w', opt='n')

Vector histogram display:

fig, ax = graphics.histvec_disp(ds, opt='n')

docs.title: Extract a rectangular region (PIVMAT-style extractf)
docs.text:
Extract a rectangle defined in physical units:

sub = ds.piv.extractf([0.0, 0.0, 10.0, 5.0], 'phys')  # [x1, y1, x2, y2]

Or extract using mesh indices (MATLAB-like 1-based, inclusive):

sub = ds.piv.extractf([10, 5, 50, 40], 'mesh')

Optionally retrieve the effective mesh rectangle after clamping:

sub, mesh_rect = ds.piv.extractf([0.0, 0.0, 10.0, 5.0], 'phys', return_rect=True)

docs.title: Matrix correlation along one direction
docs.text:
Compute a PIVMAT-like correlation map (returns a DataArray with a lag dimension):

cu = ds.piv.corrm(variable='u', dim='x')
cv = ds.piv.corrm(variable='v', dim='y', half=True)

docs.title: Spatial correlation function and integral scales
docs.text:
Compute the 1D correlation function f(r) and integral scales:

cor = ds.piv.corrf(variable='u', dim='x', normalize=True)

The result is an xarray.Dataset with:

  • cor['r']: separation length
  • cor['f']: correlation function
  • scalar diagnostics: isinf, r5/is5, r2/is2, r1/is1, r0/is0

docs.title: Butterworth filtering (PIVMAT-style bwfilterf)
docs.text:
Apply a low-pass Butterworth filter in Fourier space:

ds_low = ds.piv.bwfilterf(filtsize=3.0, order=8.0, mode='low', trunc=True)

Apply a high-pass filter:

ds_high = ds.piv.bwfilterf(filtsize=3.0, order=8.0, mode='high')

docs.title: PIVMAT-compatible option wrapper
docs.text:
If you prefer PIVMAT-like option strings:

ds_high2 = ds.piv.bwfilterf_pm(3.0, 8.0, 'high', 'trunc')

docs.title: Spatial convolution filtering (PIVMAT-style filterf)
docs.text:
Apply a Gaussian convolution filter (NaN-aware). Use 'same' to keep the same size:

ds_smooth = ds.piv.filterf(1.0, 'gauss', 'same')

Or omit 'same' to get Matlab conv2(...,'valid') behavior (smaller field):

ds_smooth_valid = ds.piv.filterf(1.0, 'gauss')

docs.title: Batch processing over filename series (PIVMAT-style batchf)
docs.text:
batchf expands bracket patterns (a safe subset of PIVMAT's expandstr) and processes files one-by-one.

from pivpy.io import batchf

# Apply an accessor method by name
results = batchf(
    'pivpy/data/day2/day2a00500[0:5].T000.D000.P003.H001.L.vec',
    'averf',
)

You can also pass a callable:

def mean_speed(ds):
    return ((ds['u'] ** 2 + ds['v'] ** 2) ** 0.5).mean().item()

speeds = batchf('pivpy/data/day2/day2a00500[0:5].*.vec', mean_speed)

docs.title: Check for updates on PyPI
docs.text:
PIVPy can compare the installed version against the latest PyPI version:

import pivpy

res = pivpy.check_update(verbose=True)
# res.status:
# 0 = server unavailable
# 1 = up-to-date
# 2 = update available
# 3 = installed version newer than PyPI

docs.title: Notes on running headless
docs.text:
If you run tests or scripts on a machine without a display, set a non-interactive Matplotlib backend:

MPLBACKEND=Agg uv run pytest -q

docs.title: PIVPy Visualization & Animations
docs.text: PIVPy provides an intuitive, publication-ready visualization and animation suite for particle image velocimetry (PIV) vector fields and derived flow diagnostics.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The primary visualization entry points are:

  • pivpy.graphics.plot (and xarray.Dataset.piv.plot): High-level zero-effort publication-quality figure combining smooth scalar fluid contours (vorticity, speed, KE), streamlines, auto-scaled vector arrows, colorbar, and reference arrow key.
  • pivpy.graphics.animate (and xarray.Dataset.piv.animate): High-performance interactive and exportable flow animations using in-place vector artist updates (quiver.set_UVC) and dynamic fluid gradient tracking.
  • pivpy.graphics.quiver / xarray.Dataset.piv.quiver: Clean vector quiver plots with subsampling, scaling, and custom arrow colors.
  • pivpy.graphics.streamplot / xarray.Dataset.piv.streamplot: Flow streamlines tracing instantaneous flow trajectories.
  • pivpy.graphics.showf / xarray.Dataset.piv.showf: PIVMat-compatible multi-purpose field viewer.
  • pivpy.graphics.to_movie / xarray.Dataset.piv.to_movie: Direct batch movie file exporter for time-series datasets.

docs.title: Try it live
docs.text: The two cells below run right here in the page (via marimo + Pyodide) -- drag the slider and the plot redraws immediately.

docs.title: High-Level Plotting (ds.piv.plot)
docs.text:
Zero-effort publication-grade visualization out-of-the-box:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pivpy.pivpy  # registers Dataset.piv accessor
from pivpy import synthetic

# Load data or generate a synthetic 2D turbulence field
ds = synthetic.multivortex(n_frames=1, n=128, n_vortices=8, two_d=True, seed=42)

# Render with one call
fig, ax = ds.piv.plot()
plt.show()

{ width="80%" }

docs.title: Customizing Visual Layers
docs.text:
All layers (background contour, quiver arrows, streamlines, color limits, Gaussian smoothing) can be tailored or toggled:

# Velocity magnitude background with vectors only (no streamlines)
fig, ax = ds.piv.plot(
    background="mag",       # 'vorticity' (default), 'mag', 'ke', 'divergence', or None
    streamlines=False,      # toggle flow streamlines
    quiver=True,            # toggle velocity vectors
    blur=1.5,               # Gaussian smoothing sigma for smooth fluid contours
    arrow_scale=0.75,       # custom vector arrow scale
    arrow_color="#1a1a1a",  # custom arrow color
    arrow_alpha=0.8,        # arrow transparency
    title="Velocity Magnitude & Vectors",
)

docs.title: How PIVPy Animations Work
docs.text:
Traditional Matplotlib animations that redraw the axes on every frame can be slow and cause visual flickering. PIVPy implements high-performance artist updating techniques:

  1. In-place Vector Updates: The velocity quiver artist is initialized once on frame 0. For subsequent time steps, vector components are updated directly in-place via quiver.set_UVC(U, V) without recreating artists.
  2. Dynamic Smooth Scalar Fields: Background fluid scalar fields (such as evolving vorticity or kinetic energy) are rendered as Gouraud-shaded meshes and updated via mesh.set_array(...) across frames.
  3. Consistent Global Scaling: Color limits (clim) and arrow scaling are calculated robustly across the entire dataset duration, preventing colorbar jumps and flickering between frames.

docs.title: Quickstart Animation Example
docs.text:
import pivpy.pivpy
from pivpy import synthetic

# 1. Generate or load time-series flow data (e.g. interacting vortex pair)
ds = synthetic.vortex_pair(n_frames=24, n=128)

# 2. Create the animation object
anim = ds.piv.animate(interval=80)

# 3. Save as GIF or MP4
anim.save("vortex_pair.gif", writer="pillow")

{ width="80%" }

docs.title: Displaying in Jupyter and Marimo Notebooks
docs.text:
In interactive environments, display the animation inline as HTML5 video or interactive JS player:

from IPython.display import HTML

anim = ds.piv.animate(interval=80)
HTML(anim.to_jshtml())

docs.title: Tuning Animation Parameters
docs.text:
The pivpy.graphics.animate function exposes fine-grained control:

anim = ds.piv.animate(
    background="vorticity",          # 'vorticity', 'mag', 'ke', 'divergence', or variable name
    quiver=True,                     # overlay velocity vectors
    blur=1.5,                        # Gaussian smoothing sigma
    skip=8,                          # arrow subsampling step (e.g. every 8th vector)
    arrow_width=0.007,               # shaft width of vector arrows
    arrow_color="#1a1a1a",           # arrow color
    arrow_alpha=0.75,                # arrow opacity
    cmap="RdBu_r",                   # colormap for background
    interval=60,                     # delay between frames in milliseconds (~16 fps)
    repeat=True,                     # loop animation
    title_fmt="Vortex Interaction (t = {t:.2f} s)", # custom dynamic title
)

docs.title: Saving High-Quality Videos (MP4 / GIF)
docs.text:
You can export animations using Pillow (GIF) or FFmpeg (MP4 / WebM):

from matplotlib.animation import FFMpegWriter, PillowWriter

# High-quality GIF
anim.save("flow.gif", writer=PillowWriter(fps=15))

# High-definition MP4 (requires ffmpeg installed)
anim.save("flow.mp4", writer=FFMpegWriter(fps=24, metadata=dict(artist="PIVPy"), bitrate=2000))

docs.title: Batch Video Export (ds.piv.to_movie)
docs.text:
For very large datasets or out-of-core file sequences on disk where holding full animations in memory is undesirable, use pivpy.graphics.to_movie or pivpy.graphics.imvectomovie:

# In-memory time series
ds.piv.to_movie("output.mp4", background="vorticity", fps=15)

# Out-of-core disk file sequences
from pivpy.graphics import imvectomovie
imvectomovie("data_run_*.vec", output="run_movie.mp4", background="mag", fps=20)

docs.text:
